title: Existence, counting and majority
cap: The formula a or b has three satisfying assignments out of four. The chapter's bipartite matrix has exactly three perfect matchings, whereas its determinant is negative one.
tex:
\(\begin{array}{c|cccc}
(a,b)&00&01&10&11\\\hline
a\lor b&0&1&1&1
\end{array}\)\par
Exists? YES. Count? 3. Strict majority? YES (\(3>2\)).\par
\(\displaystyle A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\qquad
\begin{array}{l}
\text{permitted permutations:}\\
(1,2,3),(1,3,2),(2,1,3)
\end{array}\)\par
\(\operatorname{perm}(A)=3,\quad\det(A)=-1.\)\par
The matrix is the edge-incidence description of the bipartite graph;
each listed permutation selects one 1 per row and column.

title: Randomness and one-sided errors
cap: Acceptance ranges for RP, coRP and BPP; exact evaluations of t(t-1) modulo seven on four inputs. Two zero values produce a one-half miss probability.
tex:
\(\begin{array}{c|cc}
&\text{NO acceptance}&\text{YES acceptance}\\ \hline
RP&0&[1/2,1]\\
coRP&[0,1/2]&1\\
BPP&[0,1/3]&[2/3,1]
\end{array}\)\par
\(\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
t&0&1&2&3\\\hline
t(t-1)\pmod 7&0&0&2&6
\end{array}\)\par
Uniform trial: probability of missing the nonzero polynomial \(=1/2\).\par
Independent \(r\) trials: miss probability \(2^{-r}\) for this example.
This is error probability, not expected runtime.

title: Same parity, different dependency depth
cap: Eight-bit parity uses seven XOR gates in both a chain and a balanced tree. Sequential depth is seven; balanced depth is three.
tex:
Sequential chain:\par
\(\bigl((((((b_1\oplus b_2)\oplus b_3)\oplus b_4)
\oplus b_5)\oplus b_6)\oplus b_7\bigr)\oplus b_8\)\par
\(W=7,\ D=7\).\par
Balanced dependency tree:\par
\(\begin{array}{cccc}
b_1\oplus b_2&b_3\oplus b_4&b_5\oplus b_6&b_7\oplus b_8\\
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\searrow\quad\swarrow}&
\multicolumn{2}{c}{\searrow\quad\swarrow}\\
\multicolumn{2}{c}{u_1\oplus u_2}&
\multicolumn{2}{c}{u_3\oplus u_4}\\
\multicolumn{4}{c}{\searrow\qquad\swarrow}\\
\multicolumn{4}{c}{v_1\oplus v_2}
\end{array}\)\par
\(W=7,\ D=3\). Rows represent rounds, not measured wall time.

title: Parameter dependence changes the exponent
cap: Comparison of example upper bounds 2^k n squared and n^k for several input sizes and parameter values. For fixed k, the first exponent remains two.
tex:
\(\begin{array}{rr|rr}
n&k&2^k n^2&n^k\\\hline
16&2&1024&256\\
16&4&4096&65536\\
64&2&16384&4096\\
64&4&65536&16777216
\end{array}\)\par
\(2^k n^2:\) fixed exponent in \(n\), parameter factor \(2^k\).\par
\(n^k:\) exponent depends on \(k\).\par
These are example upper bounds, not measured times or lower bounds.
FPT does not mean uniformly faster for every finite \(n,k\).

title: Matching lower bound and approximation
cap: A maximal matching M provides lower bound |M|; its endpoints give a cover of cost twice |M|. A star attains ratio two.
tex:
\(\boxed{|M|\ \le\ \mathrm{OPT}\ \le\ |S|=2|M|}\)\par
\(\begin{array}{ccc}
 &c&\\
\swarrow&\downarrow&\searrow\\
a&b&d
\end{array}\)\par
Star example: edges \(ca,cb,cd\). Choose \(M=\{ca\}\).\par
Endpoint cover \(S=\{c,a\}\) has size 2;
optimum \(\{c\}\) has size 1.\par
A matching lower bound is valid because disjoint edges require
distinct covering vertices. No maximum matching is needed.

title: Probability mass is not runtime contribution
cap: One input has exponential extra delay. Uniform distribution gives it probability 2^-n and expected extra delay one; a point mass gives exponential expectation.
tex:
\(\begin{array}{l|cc}
&\text{uniform}&\text{point mass}\\\hline
\Pr(\text{slow input})&2^{-n}&1\\
\text{extra delay}&2^n&2^n\\
\text{expected extra delay}&1&2^n
\end{array}\)\par
\(\mathbb{E}[\text{extra delay}]
=\Pr(\text{slow input})\cdot 2^n\).\par
The worst-case delay is unchanged. The distribution changes the expectation.
This deliberately slow algorithm decides an easy language.

title: Computable translators versus oracle access
cap: HALT and ACCEPT are mutually many-one reducible; complement HALT cannot many-one reduce to HALT but is Turing equivalent by one query and negation.
tex:
\(\mathrm{HALT}\ \underset{\le_m}{\overset{\le_m}{\rightleftarrows}}\ \mathrm{ACCEPT}\)\par
The translators produce finite wrapper code; they do not run the
unbounded simulation.\par
\(\overline{\mathrm{HALT}}\not\le_m\mathrm{HALT}\)\par
Otherwise recognizability of HALT would transfer to its complement.\par
\(\overline{\mathrm{HALT}}\le_T\mathrm{HALT}\), and
\(\mathrm{HALT}\le_T\overline{\mathrm{HALT}}\).\par
One oracle membership query followed by negation suffices.
This is not an implementable halting decider.

title: Bounded and unbounded quantifiers
cap: NP certificates have a polynomial bound on length; halting uses an unbounded time witness; totality quantifies over all inputs and then some finite halting time.
tex:
\(\begin{array}{l|l}
NP&\exists w,\ |w|\le p(|x|): R(x,w)\\
\Sigma^0_1\text{ example}&\exists t:\ H(e,x,t)\\
\Pi^0_2\text{ example}&\forall x\,\exists t:\ H(e,x,t)
\end{array}\)\par
In NP, \(R\) is polynomial-time decidable.
For the halting predicate \(H\), \(t\) ranges over all naturals.\par
\(\mathbf 0<_T\mathbf 0'<_T\mathbf 0''<_T\cdots\)\par
Strict oracle jumps measure computability, not time.
The arithmetical hierarchy is not the polynomial hierarchy.
